transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I suppose I came in because I feel like I’m just always… moving, if that makes sense. Even on a quiet day, I’ll start with the garden club list, then I’m over at my knitting bag, then I remember I have travel papers to sort, and before I know it I haven’t really finished any one of them.

It’s funny, the garden club has this whole thing about who brings refreshments, and I keep meaning to organize it properly, but then I see the yarn sitting there and—anyway. It’s just that I feel like I’m bouncing from one thing to the next all the time.
Have you ever experienced periods where you felt unusually upbeat, energetic, or even invincible, where you needed less sleep but still had lots of energy?

I don’t think so… not like invincible, no. I have days where I’m busy and I get wound up, like if I’m preparing for a garden club meeting and suddenly I’m sorting papers at midnight, but that’s more me getting sidetracked than feeling unusually powerful or anything.

Sleep… well, I’ve never really thought of it that way. I don’t recall needing hardly any sleep and still feeling wonderful the next day. If I stay up, I usually notice it.
Do you ever find it hard to sit still or relax, even when you know you should take a break?

Yes, I do. If I sit still too long, I get this sort of stirred-up feeling inside, like I ought to get up and straighten a pile of papers or check whether I left something out in the kitchen.

Even when I’m supposed to be relaxing, I’ll think, “Oh, I should just fix that one thing,” and then I’m up. It’s not always a big thing, just… sitting there can feel uncomfortable after a while.
Do you often find that you get easily distracted by things around you, even when you're trying to focus on a task?

Oh yes, that happens to me. I’ll be trying to do one thing, and if someone’s talking in the next room, my mind just sort of goes over there instead.

Or even a car going by the window—then I’m looking out, thinking who that might be, and then I’ve lost what I was doing. It’s a bit silly sometimes, because I’ll have papers in front of me and suddenly I’m thinking about the neighbor’s driveway or whether the mail came. So yes, I do get pulled away pretty easily.
Do you ever feel like you lose interest in things you used to enjoy, like your garden club or knitting, even for a period of time?

I’m not sure I’d say I lose interest exactly. I still like the garden club, and knitting too, though sometimes the knitting bag sits by my chair for ages because I mean to pick it up and then I notice something else needs doing.

The garden club can be a lot of little details, you know—who’s bringing the coffee, whether the church hall has enough chairs, and then I start thinking about the begonias Mrs. Harris brought last spring… but no, I don’t think I’ve had a spell where I just didn’t care about it anymore. At least not that I’ve noticed.
Do you often find yourself acting on impulse, like saying or doing something before thinking it through, or making decisions suddenly without considering the consequences?

Yes, I suppose I do sometimes. My husband tells me I cut him off before he’s finished talking, and I don’t mean to be rude, truly. It’s more that if I don’t say the thought right then, I’m afraid it’ll just fly out of my head.

It happens at group planning too, like when we’re organizing something and someone’s talking through the details. I’ll jump in with my bit before they’re done, because I’m worried I’ll forget it. Then afterward I think, “Oh dear, I should have waited.”
Have there been times when you felt down, sad, or hopeless for most of the day, even when there wasn’t a clear reason for it?

I don’t know that I’d say hopeless, no. I mean, everybody has a gloomy day now and then, don’t they? Especially when the weather sits gray for too long—my mother used to say a person can’t think straight without a bit of sun, and I do think there’s something to that.

But most of the day, for no clear reason… I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed it that way. I might feel a bit low if plans fall through or if I’ve misplaced something important, but that’s more frustration than anything, I think.

Can you describe a time when you had to stay still or slow down—like during a meeting or while watching a movie? Did you feel unusually restless or as if you couldn’t control the urge to move or do something?

Oh yes, I do get that way if I have to sit too long. Like at a meeting, I’ll start out fine, but after a while I get this sort of stirred-up feeling inside, like I need to stand up and straighten the table or go check whether the kettle’s been turned off or something.

It’s not even that anything needs doing, necessarily. I just feel like I ought to move. During a movie I can sit if it’s really good, but even then I’ll find myself wanting to get up and fuss with something. My husband can sit through the whole thing like a stone, but I start thinking, “I should just go tidy that stack of papers,” and then I’m half out of the chair before I know it.
When did you first start noticing these feelings of restlessness or difficulty focusing? Were they something you experienced even as a child, like before you were 12 years old?

Oh, yes, that goes way back. Grade school, even. My teachers used to tell my mother I was bright, but scattered — that was the word they used a lot, I think. I was always losing papers, or talking before I was meant to, and wiggling around in my seat instead of finishing my work.

My mother kept a little drawer with school notes in it, actually — funny what you remember — and she’d get so exasperated because I’d come home without the worksheet or with someone else’s paper tucked in my book. But yes, before I was 12, certainly.
